summary: The paper has no estimated regression or formal theoretical model. Its only model content is two proposed specifications in Section 6.3: an ordered latent-variable model of date precision (eq. 1) and a triple-difference housing-listing model (eq. 2). The audit found several problems in how eq. (2) is specified and interpreted. The outcome is defined as both an indicator and a price. Near_j has no project index. The triple-difference model omits the lower-order Near×Attention term. The claim that misdating biases results toward zero ignores differential error. Restricting to precisely dated projects removes most variation in the Attention variable. The interpretation of eq. (1) also overlooks a mechanical link between attention and precision. Separately, the Table 9 classification rule contradicts its own example, and three text-table or definition inconsistencies were found (Figure 1 numerator unit, Stord footnote, Q1 2024 vs January–April gap). Tables 3, 4 and 8, the Table 6 counts and the Table 5 geometry were cross-checked and are consistent within rounding. The structured table CSV/markdown was avoided per parser-quality guidance; page text was used.

findings.finding_summary: Eq. (2) defines Y_jpt as an indicator for a cycling mention but allows the same Y_jpt to be a listing price, so the outcome's type and the sign hypotheses (θ>0, δ>0) are not defined for the price case.

findings.claim_text: Y_jpt indicates that listing j near project p in month t mentions cycling (any type, or each type separately; alternatively, its price).
findings.evidence_summary: The text says Y_jpt 'indicates that' a listing mentions cycling, a binary variable. It then adds 'alternatively, its price' as another value of the same symbol. A price is continuous (levels or logs unspecified), so the interpretation of θ and δ, the estimator (linear probability vs price regression) and the hypotheses θ>0 and δ>0 differ by outcome. The paper does not distinguish them. The equation is labelled an example specification, so this is a definitional ambiguity, not a computational error.

Being in the inner band is a property of a listing–project pair. If a listing lies near one project and far from another, Near_j is not well defined. findings.finding_summary: Eq. (2) includes the triple interaction Near×Post×Attention without the Near_j×Attention_p lower-order term, which neither fixed effect absorbs, so δ is not clearly the differential post-opening effect of attention.

location.text_quote: The hypotheses are θ > 0 and δ > 0: openings increase mentions of cycling nearby, and

findings.claim_text: The hypotheses are θ > 0 and δ > 0: openings increase mentions of cycling nearby, and more so when the opening is well known locally.
findings.evidence_summary: The fixed effects are area α_a(j) and project-by-month λ_pt. λ_pt absorbs Post_pt, Attention_p and Post_pt×Attention_p, because all three vary only at project-month level. α_a(j) absorbs Near_j only if Near_j is constant within area, and it never absorbs Near_j×Attention_p. The displayed model contains Near×Post and Near×Post×Attention but not the Near_j×Attention_p term, so a pre-existing difference in cycling mentions between near and far listings that varies with Attention_p loads onto δ. Interpreting δ>0 as 'more so when the opening is well known' needs that term or an explicit assumption that it is zero. The paper calls these specifications examples, so this is a specification gap to fix.

findings.finding_summary: The statement that date misclassification 'could bias the results toward zero' does not follow for eq. (2), because misclassification that is larger for low-Attention projects would attenuate θ differently across Attention and so bias δ, possibly away from zero.

findings.claim_text: Some listings could be assigned to the wrong side of the opening if projects with less attention are dated less precisely. This could bias the results toward zero.
findings.evidence_summary: The premise is that misdating of Post_pt is related to Attention_p, which is differential measurement error. Classical attenuation of θ is plausible. In eq. (2), however, δ is the coefficient on Near×Post×Attention. If the effect is attenuated more for low-Attention projects, the estimated interaction rises mechanically, so δ>0 could appear even when the true effect does not depend on attention. The sentence refers generally to 'the results', but the sign and direction of the bias on the heterogeneity coefficient is not toward zero. The text does not distinguish θ from δ.

findings.finding_summary: The proposed remedy of restricting eq. (2) to precisely dated projects conflicts with the paper's own counts: most day-dated projects are ones with a reported ceremony, so the sample would have little variation in Attention and δ would be poorly identified.

findings.claim_text: If date precision is related to attention, model (2) should only use precisely dated projects.
findings.evidence_summary: The paper reports that of 44 projects, 18 have a reported ceremony and 17 of those can be dated to the day, versus 2 of the 26 without a ceremony. So 17 of the 19 day-dated projects have a ceremony. If 'precisely dated' means day precision and Attention is measured by ceremony, the restricted sample contains almost no no-ceremony projects, and the Near×Post×Attention coefficient δ rests on about two projects. The restriction also selects on the variable (Attention) whose effect δ is meant to estimate. If month precision is included (29 projects in Table 6), variation may be larger, but the paper does not define 'precisely dated'.

findings.finding_summary: The conclusion that date precision 'depends on how much attention an opening receives' is drawn from a ceremony-versus-precision split, but the proposed Attention measures (stories, outlets, ceremony) are measured from the same articles that determine precision, so the relationship may be mechanical.

location.text_quote: depends on how much attention an opening receives.

findings.claim_text: The precision of the dates is not random but depends on how much attention an opening receives, and eq. (1) tests this.
findings.evidence_summary: In eq. (1), Attention_p is the number of distinct stories, number of outlets or a reported ceremony, and the outcome is the best date precision found in articles about the project. Projects with more articles have more chances to contain a precise date, and ceremony reports typically state the date of the ceremony. A positive β in eq. (1) would therefore be expected without any attention-dependent selection into dating. The text treats the 17/18 vs 2/26 contrast as evidence about attention. The paper presents it as a suggestion and a possible extension, so the issue is one of interpretation. Eq. (1) also uses one β for three differently scaled alternative Attention measures.

findings.finding_summary: The Appendix A.3.2 rule 'a word that fits more than one type is given the first type in the table' contradicts its own example: 'bysykkelstativ' contains 'stativ' (Parking & storage, listed before Infrastructure) yet is said to be classified as infrastructure.
findings.claim_text: If a word fits more than one type, it is given the first type in the table. For example, words containing 'bysykkel', such as 'bysykkelstativ', are counted as infrastructure.
findings.evidence_summary: Table 9 (read from page text, not the structured CSV) lists types in the order: The word 'bicycle', Proximity, Parking & storage, Leisure, Infrastructure, Other. Parking & storage includes 'stativ' (rack), which appears in 'bysykkelstativ'. Infrastructure, listed later, includes 'bysykkel'. A first-match rule would classify 'bysykkelstativ' as Parking & storage, not Infrastructure. Figure 2 lists 'bysykkelstativ' at 0.5%, and Table 8 aggregates by type. So either the stated precedence or the example is wrong, and the Infrastructure share (13.4%) and Parking & storage share (10.8%) in Table 8 depend on which was implemented. This shows a text inconsistency, not which rule was implemented.

findings.finding_summary: Section 3.1.2 states 'Only 2 of the 34 unique articles (about 6 percent) concern an opening that took place', but the numerator 2 is the number of distinct openings elsewhere described (Figure 1, Section 3.1.4), not a count of articles, so the numerator and denominator have different units.

location.text_quote: Only 2 of the 34 unique articles (about 6 percent) concern an opening that took place.

findings.claim_text: Only 2 of the 34 unique articles (about 6 percent) concern an opening that took place.
findings.evidence_summary: The arithmetic itself is consistent: 2/34 is 5.9 percent, which matches 'about 6 percent'. The problem is the unit of the numerator. Figure 1 labels the bottom bar 'Distinct openings that took place 2', and its caption says 'Only 2 of 70 search hits concern a cycling infrastructure opening that actually took place' while naming two projects (Homborsund and Stod/Steinkjer). Section 3.1.4 (page 5) says that of the five relevant articles 'only two unique openings were found. Four of the articles mention Homborsund and one Stod', and that after recoding two pre-opening Homborsund articles, three relevant articles remain. So 2 counts projects, while the sentence's denominator counts articles, and the paper's own article counts for the same concept are five (before recoding) or three (after recoding), not two. The same count of 2 is also placed over two different denominators (70 search hits in the caption, 34 unique articles in the text). The abstract's 'two actual openings' is a project count and is not affected. The paper does not define which article count (five, three or other) the 'about 6 percent' sentence is meant to report, so no corrected percentage is asserted here.
